lead: This unit explains how electrons and magnetic moments make solids conduct, switch and store magnetism. You will go from the classical electron gas to Fermi energy, bands, doped semiconductors, contacts and magnetic hysteresis. After it you can compute conductivity, Fermi energy, carrier concentrations, barrier heights and hysteresis loss, and choose soft or hard magnets for a job.
about: This unit follows the electron from a classical gas to a quantum Fermi sea, then into bands and doped semiconductors. Chapter 7.1 gets Ohm's law from drift and collisions; 7.2 replaces the classical gas with Fermi-Dirac statistics and density of states. Chapter 7.3 explains bands and doping; 7.4 computes carrier concentrations and Fermi level shifts. Chapters 7.5 and 7.6 add drift-diffusion transport and metal-semiconductor contacts. Chapters 7.7 and 7.8 turn to magnetic moments, domains, hysteresis and the choice between soft and hard magnets. The build is deliberate: each chapter removes one simplifying assumption of the previous one.

chapters.idea: A metal is a gas of free electrons whose drift under a field, interrupted by collisions, gives Ohm's law and a conductivity σ = ne²τ/m.
chapters.depth: Classical Drude model: metal = fixed positive ions plus free electron gas. Assumptions: free, independent electrons; random thermal motion; collisions with ions described by a relaxation time τ. Define drift velocity v_d, mobility μ = eτ/m, current density J = ne v_d, conductivity σ = ne²τ/m, and n = conduction electrons per unit volume. Get Ohm's law. Discuss temperature, impurity and defect scattering. Give successes (Ohm's law, order-of-magnitude Wiedemann-Franz) and failures (electronic heat capacity, ρ(T), Fermi speed). Some syllabi call this Drude theory or free electron theory of metals.

figure.title: Drude model and its test
figure.aria: A flow from metal to field, collisions and conductivity, with a dashed branch to the failures of the classical model.

chapters.example: Copper has n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³ and τ = 2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s. Take m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. (a) Find σ. (b) For a wire of area 1.0 mm² carrying 2.0 A, find the drift speed v_d. Answer: σ = ne²τ/m ≈ 6.0×10⁷ S/m; J = 2.0×10⁶ A/m²; v_d = J/(ne) ≈ 1.5×10⁻⁴ m/s.
chapters.trap: Do not use the drift speed (about 0.15 mm/s) as the speed of signal or of electrons between collisions; the Fermi speed is about 10⁶ m/s. The classical formula also does not explain ρ(T).
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: electric current and field; Unit 1: force and energy.
chapters.leave: Fermi-Dirac statistics and Fermi energy to 7.2; band structure to 7.3; magnetic moments to 7.7.

chapters.idea: Electrons obey Fermi-Dirac statistics, so only those within about k_BT of the Fermi energy take part, and the density of states controls how many states are available.
chapters.depth: Quantum free electron theory: Pauli exclusion and Fermi-Dirac distribution f(E) = 1/[1 + exp((E − E_F)/k_BT)], with k_B = Boltzmann constant. Define Fermi energy E_F as the highest occupied energy at T = 0, Fermi temperature T_F = E_F/k_B, and Fermi surface. Density of states per unit volume g(E) = (1/2π²)(2m/ħ²)<sup>3/2</sup>√E, with ħ = h/2π. At T = 0, E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)<sup>2/3</sup>. Write n = ∫ g(E)f(E)dE. Mention effective mass m* as a band parameter. Some syllabi call this Sommerfeld theory.

figure.aria: At T = 0 the occupation is a step at E/E_F = 1; at 300 K and 1000 K it rounds over a width set by k_BT.

chapters.example: Copper has n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³. Take m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg and ħ = 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J s. Find E_F and T_F. Answer: E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)<sup>2/3</sup> ≈ 1.1×10⁻¹⁸ J ≈ 7.0 eV; T_F = E_F/k_B ≈ 8.2×10⁴ K, with k_B = 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K.
chapters.trap: g(E) is not constant; it rises as √E. E_F is a T = 0 energy, not k_BT, and it is not the energy of the highest-speed electron at room temperature.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6: particle in a box and wave function; 7.1.
chapters.leave: Band gaps and doping to 7.3; transport to 7.5.

chapters.idea: A periodic lattice turns free-electron energies into allowed bands separated by gaps; doping chooses whether electrons or holes carry the current.
chapters.depth: Origin of bands from a periodic potential; Bloch theorem (qualitative); Kronig-Penney model (qualitative); E-k diagram; one-dimensional zone scheme; band gap. Compare metals, insulators and semiconductors. Intrinsic semiconductor: n = p = n_i, with n_i² = N_C N_V exp(−E_g/k_BT); N_C and N_V are effective densities of states; E_g is the band gap. Extrinsic: donor gives n-type, acceptor gives p-type; Fermi level moves toward the majority-carrier band. Some syllabi call this band theory of solids.

figure.aria: Schematic direct-gap E-k diagram with a gap of 1.1 eV; the flat line is the Fermi level in an n-type sample.

chapters.example: Silicon has E_g = 1.1 eV, N_C = 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³ and N_V = 1.0×10¹⁹ cm⁻³ at 300 K. Find n_i at 300 K. Take k_BT = 0.0259 eV. Answer: n_i² = N_C N_V exp(−E_g/k_BT) ≈ 1.0×10²⁰ cm⁻⁶; n_i ≈ 1.0×10¹⁰ cm⁻³.
chapters.trap: Intrinsic does not mean no carriers; n_i is very temperature-sensitive. Do not put the donor level at the Fermi level; donors sit just below E_C.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6: particle in a box; 7.2 Fermi-Dirac statistics.
chapters.leave: Carrier concentration formulas to 7.4; drift and diffusion to 7.5; contacts to 7.6.

chapters.idea: Doping fixes the majority carrier density; Fermi-Dirac statistics then fix the minority density, the Fermi level and the temperature behaviour.
chapters.depth: Carrier concentrations from Fermi-Dirac statistics: n = N_C exp[−(E_C−E_F)/k_BT] and p = N_V exp[−(E_F−E_V)/k_BT], with E_C and E_V the band edges. Mass action: n p = n_i². Charge neutrality. N-type: n ≈ N_D and E_C−E_F = k_BT ln(N_C/N_D). P-type: p ≈ N_A and E_F−E_V = k_BT ln(N_V/N_A). Temperature regimes: freeze-out, extrinsic, intrinsic. Keep to non-degenerate doping.

figure.title: Doping sets carrier density
figure.aria: Doping branches into donor and acceptor paths, giving n-type and p-type carrier densities that meet at the mass-action relation.

chapters.example: A Si sample has N_D = 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ at 300 K. Take N_C = 2.8×10¹⁹ cm⁻³, n_i = 1.0×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and k_BT = 0.0259 eV. Assume full ionization. Find n, p and E_C−E_F. Answer: n ≈ 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³; p = n_i²/n ≈ 1.0×10⁴ cm⁻³; E_C−E_F = k_BT ln(N_C/n) ≈ 0.21 eV.
chapters.trap: Do not use n = N_D when N_D is comparable to n_i, or at high temperature when intrinsic carriers take over. Keep cm⁻³ and m⁻³ separate.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 bands and intrinsic carriers; 7.2 Fermi-Dirac statistics.
chapters.leave: Transport to 7.5; junction band bending to 7.6.

chapters.idea: Carriers move by drift in a field and by diffusion down a concentration gradient; the total current is the sum, and the Einstein relation links the two coefficients.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in first year. One-dimensional steady state: drift J_n = n e μ_n E and J_p = p e μ_p E; diffusion J_n = e D_n dn/dx and J_p = −e D_p dp/dx; total J = J_n + J_p; conductivity σ = e(n μ_n + p μ_p); mobility v_d = μE; Einstein relation D/μ = k_BT/e. No continuity equation derivation.

figure.title: Two currents add
figure.aria: Field drives drift and a concentration gradient drives diffusion; both meet in the total current, which uses the Einstein relation.

chapters.example: In Si at 300 K, n = 1.0×10¹⁶ cm⁻³, μ_n = 1350 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, and E = 1000 V m⁻¹. Find the electron drift current density. Answer: convert n = 1.0×10²² m⁻³ and μ_n = 0.135 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹; J_n = n e μ_n E ≈ 2.2×10⁵ A m⁻².
chapters.trap: Watch the sign of the hole diffusion current and convert cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ to m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Einstein relation uses k_BT/e ≈ 0.026 V at 300 K, not 300 K.
chapters.leave: Continuity and Poisson equations to device courses; junction barriers to 7.6.

chapters.idea: A metal-semiconductor contact is rectifying when a barrier forms and ohmic when the barrier is matched away or thin enough to tunnel.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in first year. Work function Φ_M, electron affinity χ, Schottky barrier Φ_B; depletion and band bending. For n-type, ideal Φ_B = Φ_M − χ. For p-type, Φ_B = E_g + χ − Φ_M. Ohmic contact by low barrier or heavy doping and tunnelling; I-V rectifying versus linear qualitatively.

figure.title: Schottky or ohmic
figure.aria: A metal contact with a high work function forms a Schottky barrier; heavy doping makes a thin barrier and an ohmic contact.

chapters.example: For n-Si, χ = 4.05 eV and E_C − E_F = 0.20 eV. A metal has Φ_M = 4.70 eV. Find the ideal Schottky barrier Φ_B and the built-in potential V_bi. Answer: Φ_B = Φ_M − χ = 0.65 eV; V_bi = Φ_B − (E_C − E_F)/e = 0.45 V.
chapters.trap: The n-type formula Φ_B = Φ_M − χ does not apply unchanged to p-type; there Φ_B = E_g + χ − Φ_M. An ohmic contact is not a zero-barrier contact; heavy doping makes a thin barrier that tunnels.
chapters.leave: Detailed diode I-V and MOS devices to electronics courses.

chapters.idea: Atomic moments make diamagnets oppose, paramagnets weakly follow and ferromagnets strongly align in domains.
chapters.depth: Magnetic dipole moment m; magnetization M = magnetic moment per unit volume; field H; B = μ0(H + M); susceptibility χ = M/H; relative permeability μ_r = 1 + χ. Diamagnetic: small negative χ, induced orbital currents oppose H. Paramagnetic: small positive χ, Curie law χ = C/T. Ferromagnetic: domains, large χ, saturation, Curie temperature T_C; above T_C it becomes paramagnetic. Mention antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic briefly. Some syllabi call this magnetic classification.

figure.aria: Diamagnetic magnetization is small and negative; paramagnetic is small and positive; ferromagnetic rises steeply and saturates.

chapters.example: A paramagnetic salt has χ = 1.5×10⁻⁴ at 300 K. Find the Curie constant C and χ at 200 K. Answer: C = χT = 0.045 K; χ(200 K) = C/T = 2.25×10⁻⁴.
chapters.trap: Diamagnetism is present in every material but often masked. Ferromagnetic χ is not a constant; it depends on field and history. Do not use χ = C/T below T_C for a ferromagnet.

chapters.idea: The hysteresis loop area is the energy lost per unit volume per cycle; soft magnets have narrow loops, hard magnets wide loops.
chapters.depth: B-H loop: saturation, retentivity B_r, coercivity H_c. Loop area ∮H dB = energy loss per unit volume per cycle. Soft magnetic materials: narrow loop, low H_c, high μ, small loss, used in transformer cores and inductors. Hard magnetic materials: wide loop, high H_c and B_r, used in permanent magnets. Mention eddy-current loss and lamination.

figure.aria: Schematic B-H loops: the soft loop is narrow and the hard loop is wide; the area enclosed is the hysteresis loss.

chapters.example: A transformer core of volume 500 cm³ is taken through a hysteresis loop of area 250 J/m³ per cycle at 50 Hz. Find the hysteresis power loss. Answer: volume = 5.0×10⁻⁴ m³; energy per cycle = 250×5.0×10⁻⁴ = 0.125 J; power = 0.125×50 = 6.25 W.
chapters.trap: The loop area is energy per unit volume per cycle. Multiply by volume and frequency to get power; do not treat the area as watts.
chapters.leave: Magnetic anisotropy and domain theory to advanced courses; transformer design to electrical engineering.
